readings.title: A New England Girlhood: two stolen pennies (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Follow how a grown writer remembers the feelings of a small child who did wrong.
readings.focus: Five-year-old Lucy takes two cents to buy a candy toy, and her conscience will not let her keep them.
readings.context: Lucy Larcom (1824–1893), a poet and teacher, grew up in a large family in Beverly, Massachusetts, a seaport near Salem. Her father, once a sea captain, kept a shop. A New England Girlhood (1889) is her memoir of her childhood, written when she was in her sixties. Her parents were Puritans, strict Protestants. Ananias and Sapphira are a couple in the Bible who fell dead after lying; the Eighth Commandment is “Thou shalt not steal.” An equestrian is a horseback rider; purloined means stolen; austere means stern; a defaulter steals money trusted to him. Tyburn was a place in London where criminals were once hanged. The 1889 printing has “shop-widow,” a misprint for “shop-window.”
readings.contentNote: The child imagines being jailed and hanged for her theft, remembering a story-book boy hanged for stealing.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, “Naughty Children and Fairy Tales,” from the opening through the sugar horseback rider; opens “ALTHOUGH the children of an earlier time heard a great deal of theological discussion…”; closes “…enough when some other child had bought him and left his place in the window vacant.”.

questions.prompt: How is Lucy’s playmate, who “only kind of said no,” different from Lucy?
facilitatorNotes: The playmate tells a plain lie and calls it only “kind-of” lying; Lucy cannot lie deliberately, though she has other temptations. The contrast prepares for Lucy’s own wrongdoing.
evidence: Oh, I only kind of said no.
I could not deliberately lie, but I had my own temptations

questions.prompt: How does Lucy take the extra money so that her father does not notice?
facilitatorNotes: His back is turned at his desk, and she counts four cents aloud, as usual, while really taking six.
evidence: I counted out four cents aloud, but took six

questions.prompt: What happens in the field? Did the pennies really burn, or is Larcom describing a feeling?
facilitatorNotes: The sky seems to darken and the coins seem red-hot, so she drops them and runs. It is her guilt, felt so strongly that it seems physical. When she later looks for them and cannot find them, she gives credit to her “good angel.”
evidence: those two pennies began to burn through my hand
But my good angel hid them from me; I never found them.

questions.prompt: Lucy never confesses. What did that cost her, and what did the whole experience teach her?
facilitatorNotes: She carried shame for months and dreamed of jail and the gallows; she says confessing would have made her happier. She never again wanted to take what was not hers, and came to hate the sight of the sugar rider. Readers may discuss whether the guilt was too heavy for so small a wrong.
evidence: I was too much of a coward to confess my fault to my father
I should have been a much happier child

readings.title: A New England Girlhood: the blue wall and the shore (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Notice how a child’s mistakes and discoveries teach her what is alive and what is huge.
readings.focus: Lucy’s sister shows her the sea at sunrise, and Lucy explores the shore alone.
readings.context: Lucy Larcom (1824–1893), a poet and teacher, grew up in a large family in Beverly, Massachusetts, a seaport near Salem. Her father, once a sea captain, kept a shop. A New England Girlhood (1889) is her memoir of her childhood, written when she was in her sixties. The sister here is one of Lucy’s older sisters, who told her fairy tales and cared for her like a second mother. A garret is an attic; a pumpkin sweeting is a sweet apple; Captain Cook was a famous English explorer; mucilage is glue; sea-lovage and beach-peas are seaside plants. At the end, Larcom uses religious words: “Law” (the commandments) and “Gospel” (the good news of Jesus).
readings.contentNote: Lucy accidentally kills a starfish and some shellfish by carrying them home, and some children torment horseshoe crabs.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, “Naughty Children and Fairy Tales,” from the sister who toughened herself through the tide; opens “This sister, though only just entering her teens, was toughening herself by all sorts of…”; closes “…belong together. "The sea is His, and He made it: and His hands formed the dry land."”.

questions.prompt: What did Lucy think the sea was when she first saw it? Why might she have thought so that morning?
facilitatorNotes: An immense blue wall, because she had never seen it, there was no sail in sight, and the high tide was so calm that there was hardly a ripple.
evidence: what looked to me like an immense blue wall
So you did not know it was the sea, little girl!

questions.prompt: Why did Lucy’s sister sleep on a sea-chest and visit the graveyard before dawn? What kind of person was she?
facilitatorNotes: She was “toughening herself” for whatever her life as a woman might bring, and was brave enough to look for ghosts. She was also playful, bringing back apples and planning surprises for her little sister.
evidence: toughening herself by all sorts of unnecessary hardships
to see if there were any ghosts there

questions.prompt: What did Lucy learn from the starfish and the shells? How did she feel?
facilitatorNotes: That they were living creatures. She hung the starfish to dry without thinking it was alive, and her conscience hurt; after finding dead snails in her shells, she took only empty ones. She would not turn horseshoe crabs over, thinking it “wicked.”
evidence: not thinking of him as a living creature
This made me careful to pick up only the empty ones
I thought it must be wicked.

questions.prompt: The tide seemed to laugh, “I am coming!” What did it mean to the child, and what does the grown-up writer make of it?
facilitatorNotes: The child felt its power but “had no guess of its meaning.” The grown-up gives it a religious meaning, about Law and Gospel belonging together. Readers can decide whether the child’s wonder or the adult’s explanation speaks to them more.
evidence: laughing aloud "I am coming!"
but had no guess of its meaning

readings.title: A New England Girlhood: a town that faced the sea (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Gather details that show how far a small town reached, and notice whose stories are missing.
readings.focus: Lucy’s town is full of ships, sailors and things from far away, and of losses at sea.
readings.context: Lucy Larcom (1824–1893), a poet and teacher, grew up in a large family in Beverly, Massachusetts, a seaport near Salem. Her father, once a sea captain, kept a shop. A New England Girlhood (1889) is her memoir of her childhood, written when she was in her sixties. Canton (now Guangzhou) is in China, Smyrna (now İzmir) in Turkey, and Calcutta (now Kolkata) in India; the Grand Banks are fishing grounds off Newfoundland. A univalve is a one-part shell; an aperture is an opening; a scuttle is a hatch in a roof; the rote is the roar of surf. Ninepence and four-pence ha’penny were old British coin names still used for American money.
readings.contentNote: Larcom describes people from Asia, Africa and the Pacific in the language of her time (“swarthy complexions and un-Caucasian features”). She mentions that her great-grandfather’s family had enslaved Black people; slavery ended in Massachusetts in the 1780s. A ship’s whole crew drowns in a wreck.

excerpt.locator: Chapter V, “Old New England,” from the opening through the wreck of the Persia; opens “WHEN I first opened my eyes upon my native town, it was already nearly two hundred years…”; closes “…the next Sabbath was an event which long left its solemnity hanging over the town.”.

questions.prompt: Name three things in Lucy’s town that came from across the sea.
facilitatorNotes: Shawls and silks, shells and coral, coconuts and tropical fruits, foreign coins, parrots, songbirds and pet monkeys are all possible answers.
evidence: Green parrots went scolding and laughing down the thimbleberry hedges
We had foreign coins mixed in with our large copper cents

questions.prompt: What did the children believe about the “prop” shell? How does Larcom use its sound again later?
facilitatorNotes: They thought the ocean was trapped inside it. Later the moaning of the waves before a storm sounds like the shell, and it brings the town’s sea-tragedies to mind: the sound that was a toy becomes a warning.
evidence: I thought that the ocean was really imprisoned somewhere within that narrow aperture
with a moaning like that we heard when we listened for it in the shell

questions.prompt: What does Larcom say about Rose, Phillis and the other Black families? What does her account leave out, and whose story would you want to hear?
facilitatorNotes: They had been enslaved in her great-grandfather’s family, stayed near the old homestead after freedom, and came to sell berries and do the washing. She calls them “respected” and says they lived “on equal terms,” but also calls them “relics” and says they seemed out of place. They never speak for themselves, so readers may question her picture and wish to hear theirs.
evidence: relics of a time when even New England had not freed her slaves
They seemed pathetically out of place, although they lived among us on equal terms

questions.prompt: Why did “almost every house” have a sea-tragedy? How does the wreck of the Persia show the danger?
facilitatorNotes: So many men went to sea that many were wrecked or never came home. The Persia was nearly home, but in a snowstorm the captain probably mistook a lighthouse and steered onto the rocks.
evidence: Almost every house had its sea-tragedy.
her captain probably mistook one of the Cape Ann light-houses for that on Baker's Island

readings.title: A New England Girlhood: the belfry and the bog (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Compare two frights, and notice who acts and who helps in each.
readings.focus: Lucy is locked in a bell tower with her brother, and later saves her little sister from a bog.
readings.context: Lucy Larcom (1824–1893), a poet and teacher, grew up in a large family in Beverly, Massachusetts, a seaport near Salem. Her father, once a sea captain, kept a shop. A New England Girlhood (1889) is her memoir of her childhood, written when she was in her sixties. Her grandfather was the sexton, the caretaker of the church, who rang its bell; John was her brother. A belfry is a bell tower; to toll is to ring slowly, as for a funeral; the passing-bell was rung when someone died. Morocco is soft leather; sweet-flag and cat-tails are marsh plants.

excerpt.locator: Chapter V, “Old New England,” from the belfry adventure through the walk to the Cove; opens “My brother's vigilant care of his two youngest sisters was once the occasion to them of a…”; closes “…little sister, and I was not very soon allowed again to have her company in my rambles.”.

questions.prompt: Why did John take his two little sisters up to the belfry?
facilitatorNotes: He did not like to stay up there alone for an hour, and his grandfather forbade him to take other boys, so he got permission to bring his sisters for company.
evidence: John was social, and did not like to go up into the belfry and stay an hour or so alone

questions.prompt: How do the children get out of the locked belfry? Which part of the rescue was the cleverest?
facilitatorNotes: John shouts to a boy in the street to fetch their father; then the father and grandfather tell the children to push together, and the rusty lock gives way. Readers may choose John’s shout or the grown-ups’ simple idea.
evidence: shouted over the railing to a boy in the street
told us to push with our united strength against it

questions.prompt: Lucy, not yet six, pulls her sister from the bog. How does she explain where her strength came from? What other explanations are possible?
facilitatorNotes: She feels the “power of a giant” and believes an unseen Power used her. Others might say fear and love gave her sudden strength. Her explanation fits her faith; readers can weigh both.
evidence: I felt the power of a giant suddenly taking possession of my small frame
as if some unseen Power had taken possession of me for a moment

questions.prompt: Lucy was scolded after the bog. Was that fair?
facilitatorNotes: She was supposed to look after her sister, so the grown-ups blamed her; but the sister ran off too fast to stop, and Lucy saved her life. Most readers will think the scolding unfair, though some may see the parents’ fright behind it.
evidence: I also received a scolding for not taking better care of my little sister
she had shot from my side like an arrow from the bow

readings.title: A New England Girlhood: The Diving Bell (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Notice how a grown writer looks back at her first writing, both fondly and critically.
readings.focus: Lucy and the girls at home write their own little magazine, and her sister says she has a talent.
readings.context: Lucy Larcom (1824–1893), a poet and teacher, grew up in a large family in Beverly, Massachusetts, a seaport near Salem. Her father, once a sea captain, kept a shop. A New England Girlhood (1889) is her memoir of her childhood, written when she was in her sixties. When Lucy was about eleven, her father died and the family moved to Lowell, Massachusetts, a city of cotton mills, where her mother kept a boarding-house for mill workers and Lucy went to work in the mill. Her older sister Emilie looked after the younger girls. A diving bell is a chamber lowered underwater for divers; fortnightly means every two weeks; a maxim is a wise saying; to plagiarize is to copy someone else’s writing as your own; oblivion means being forgotten. The Lowell Offering was a real magazine written by women mill workers.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VIII, “By the River,” from the little fortnightly paper through the Improvement Circle; opens “One thing she planned for us, her younger housemates,--a dozen or so of cousins, friends,…”; closes “…Circle" grew the larger one whence issued the "Lowell Offering," a year or two later.”.

questions.prompt: Why did the girls keep the writers’ names secret? How were they found out anyway?
facilitatorNotes: Guessing who wrote each piece was part of the fun. Each writer’s habits of style gave her away: one cousin wrote stories, Lucy wrote rhymes.
evidence: It was, indeed, an important part of the fun to guess who wrote particular pieces.
After a little while, however, our mannerisms betrayed us.

questions.prompt: In Lucy’s poem “Life like a Rose,” what stage of life goes with each rose? What does the grown-up Larcom think of the poem?
facilitatorNotes: Childhood is a bud, youth a full-blown rose, and age a withered rose whose fragrance lasts. She half apologizes for it and says children usually write about growing up and old age instead of the simple things of childhood.
evidence: Its fragrance yet may last
the child's usual inclination to look forward meditatively

questions.prompt: One girl wanted to be famous “even if it was for something bad.” What did she do, and why was a scolding from Emilie punishment enough?
facilitatorNotes: She copied a long poem and passed it off as her own. The girls respected Emilie so much that her disapproval alone was enough.
evidence: she meant to be distinguished when she grew up for something, even if it was for something bad
we all thought that a reproof from Emilie was sufficient punishment

questions.prompt: Lucy thought deeds mattered more than words, but her sister told her not to neglect her talent. Who was right? Could both be?
facilitatorNotes: Lucy respected practical, capable people and did not want to be only a writer; Emilie saw a gift worth developing. Lucy did become a poet while also working all her life, so readers may argue that both were right.
evidence: certainly the world needs deeds more than it needs words
here was a talent which I had no right to neglect

readings.title: A New England Girlhood: mountain-friends (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Notice how two girls each find the other’s home wonderful or strange.
readings.focus: In the mill, Lucy meets girls from the northern hills, and longs for her own home by the sea.
readings.context: Lucy Larcom (1824–1893), a poet and teacher, grew up in a large family in Beverly, Massachusetts, a seaport near Salem. Her father, once a sea captain, kept a shop. A New England Girlhood (1889) is her memoir of her childhood, written when she was in her sixties. When Lucy was about eleven, her father died and the family moved to Lowell, Massachusetts, a city of cotton mills, where she went to work in the mill as a young girl. Many mill girls came from farms in Maine, New Hampshire and Vermont. Spools hold the spun thread; husking is stripping the leaves from ears of corn; sugar-making means boiling maple sap; checkerberry is wintergreen; “daown” and “haow” show the hill-country way of saying “down” and “how”; a commonplace is something ordinary; a headland is a point of land in the sea; the horizon is where earth and sky meet.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IX, “Mountain-Friends,” from the opening through Lucy’s stay with her married sister; opens “THE pleasure we found in making new acquaintances among our workmates arose partly from…”; closes “…soon restored my strength, and those months of quiet family life were very good for me.”.

questions.prompt: Why did Lucy find the girls from the north so interesting?
facilitatorNotes: They came from far-off places she had never seen, and they had lived among real mountains, in valleys where the sun set at four and snow cut them off for weeks.
evidence: It seemed wonderful to me to be talking with anybody who had really seen mountains and lived among them.
where the sun set at four o'clock

questions.prompt: How did the mountain girl feel about the mountains Lucy found so wonderful?
facilitatorNotes: To her they were ordinary: what she remembered was the cold and the short, dark days. A place that seems thrilling to a visitor may seem everyday, or hard, to the people who live there.
evidence: And yet here was this girl to whom it all appeared like the merest commonplace.
awful cold, sometimes; the days were so short!

questions.prompt: Lucy tried to impress her friend with stories of the sea. What happened? What did Lucy like about her friend?
facilitatorNotes: The girl was not impressed: “They don’t think much of sailors up aour way.” Lucy liked her all the more for her hill accent and the woodsy “mountain-flavor” about her. Each girl was proud of her own home.
evidence: They don't think much of sailors up aour way.
It was part of the mountain-flavor.

questions.prompt: Larcom says a birthplace is like a mother. Why did the hills “shut in” Lucy and her sisters? Do you feel tied to a place in this way?
facilitatorNotes: They grew up by the sea and were used to a wide horizon, so hills felt closed in, “body and soul.” Readers can compare with the places they come from, or with a family that has moved.
evidence: We speak of such a town, if our birthplace, as of a mother
To those who have been reared by the sea a wide horizon is a necessity, both for the mind and for the eye.

readings.title: A New England Girlhood: baby, book and housework (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Find what a girl of thirteen learned from a baby, a book and the housework.
readings.focus: Staying with her sister by the sea, Lucy cares for a baby nephew, reads Dickens and learns to keep house.
readings.context: Lucy Larcom (1824–1893), a poet and teacher, grew up in a large family in Beverly, Massachusetts, a seaport near Salem. Her father, once a sea captain, kept a shop. A New England Girlhood (1889) is her memoir of her childhood, written when she was in her sixties. When Lucy was about thirteen she left her work in the Lowell mills to stay with a married sister in Beverly. A constitution is a person’s general health; an urchin is a lively child; “feel his life in every limb” quotes the poet Wordsworth; an elegy is a poem of mourning, and “The Graves of a Household” is a sad poem by Felicia Hemans. Charles Dickens’s novel The Old Curiosity Shop came out in parts in 1840 and 1841; its heroine, Little Nell, wanders England with her grandfather and dies at the end. Despotism is the rule of a tyrant; imperious means bossy; latent means hidden; a good watcher sat up all night with the sick; compensations are rewards; vanquished means defeated.
readings.contentNote: Larcom says that neither of her nephews lived to grow up.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IX, “Mountain-Friends,” from Lucy’s baby-nephews through the beauty of work; opens “Like most young girls, I had a motherly fondness for little children, and my two…”; closes “…all day, and who will make us feel, at evening, that the day was well worth its fatigues.”.

questions.prompt: How were the two baby nephews different? Which one did Lucy look after?
facilitatorNotes: The older was delicate and thoughtful-looking and stayed close to his mother; the younger was plump and merry, and he was Lucy’s special charge.
evidence: The older one had a delicate constitution
He was my especial charge

questions.prompt: How did Lucy manage “to combine baby and book”? Why did she sometimes cry over the sleeping baby?
facilitatorNotes: She read Dickens with the baby playing at her feet or lying across her lap; she cried over the sad story of Little Nell. When the baby woke he grabbed her hair and drove the story from her head.
evidence: somehow I managed to combine baby and book.
if a tear from his nurse's eyes sometimes dropped upon his cheek as he slept

questions.prompt: Larcom calls the baby “something of a tyrant” and puts him on “the list of my girlhood’s teachers.” What could a baby teach a thirteen-year-old?
facilitatorNotes: Tenderness, patience and responsibility: caring for someone who depends on you completely. The “tyrant” is a joke about how babies rule a household.
evidence: Like all babies, he was something of a tyrant
upon the list of my girlhood's teachers.

questions.prompt: What work was every young woman expected to know? Larcom says “The beauty of work depends upon the way we meet it.” Do you agree?
facilitatorNotes: Sewing, mending, washing, ironing, cooking three meals, keeping house and nursing the sick. She found that plain sewing set her mind free for poems, and that welcoming work as a friend makes it pleasant. Readers may agree, or point out that these duties fell on girls only, and that some work is hard however you meet it.
evidence: could not make and mend and wash and iron her own clothing
The beauty of work depends upon the way we meet it
